Container.Name: codifier-mcp
Container.Overview: Self-hosted MCP server that keeps a project's rules in a SQLite registry instead of scattered Markdown files, and answers the question a chat cannot answer today: which rules am I under, right now. Rules are addressed to CONSUMERS (chats and skills) either universally or through named GROUPS plus single exceptions standing next to them, and the reading order is the breadth of the audience, so it stays correct on its own as consumers are added. The same registry also holds the project's TASKS — what is waiting for a consumer, as opposed to what binds it. History is written by database triggers, not by tool code, so a change made by hand is recorded too; nothing is ever deleted. A new rule reaches nobody until its batch is approved on the administration page, behind that page's own password and against the batch's digest, and once approved it stays until somebody ends it. ONE DATABASE PER PROJECT, all of them under one folder, declared in a text registry the owner writes; each project is addressed by an opaque code and no tool ever lists them. Access via OAuth 2.1 with GitHub login restricted to a single user, published by Tailscale Funnel.
Container.Requires: A GitHub OAuth application (free) and the Unraid Tailscale plugin with Funnel enabled. Nothing else: rules are approved from a browser on your LAN, behind the Web UI Password below. Before the service can serve anything you write one line per project in projects.txt, inside the Database directory — name, reference code, admin code — with codes you generate yourself (openssl rand -hex 12).

Config.Name: Web UI Port (published)
Config.Description: The port the administration UI is published on, on the server's own IP: you reach the page at http://SERVER-IP:9443/ like any other container of the house. This is a PORT MAPPING and the Web UI Port variable below is what the server listens on inside the container — two halves of one decision. Change one and change the other, or the page answers only inside the container and the failure looks exactly like a service that never started. The MCP port is NOT published here and must not be: it is served by the Tailscale Funnel, which runs alongside.

Config.Name: Database
Config.Description: The directory the databases live in, on the server. Inside it: projects.txt, the registry you write by hand — one line per project, `name | reference code | admin code` — and ONE FOLDER PER PROJECT, named as the project is spelled, holding that project's .db. It must be LOCAL storage — a pool or a disk — and never a network share: SQLite in WAL mode needs real file locking, and over SMB or NFS the locks are advisory at best. Backups (VACUUM INTO) are written in here too, under backup/. The databases are owned by root and readable by everyone: from the share you read them and you do not touch them, because a write by hand would bypass the triggers and break history in silence. projects.txt is the ONE exception and is 600, root only, because it carries every code in clear — the service re-imposes that mode every time it re-reads the file. Tip: give the directory a ZFS dataset of its own, so its snapshots are independent from the rest of the share.

Config.Name: App Data
Config.Description: Persistent service state: the OAuth tokens already issued (FASTMCP_HOME). It MUST live on a volume that survives container recreation — lose it and the client will ask you to authorise the connector all over again.

Config.Name: Tailscale State
Config.Description: The Tailscale node identity of this container. Lose it and the node comes back as new: the hostname changes, the Funnel needs re-authorisation and BASE_URL stops answering. One dedicated folder per container — sharing it with another container is the mistake that costs an afternoon. If Tailscale ever asks you to re-authorise during a normal update, that is not a step of the procedure: it is the symptom that this mount is missing.

Config.Name: Database Directory
Config.Description: The DIRECTORY the container sees, not a file: inside it the service finds projects.txt and one folder per project, each with that project's own database. Leave it as /db — when you move the data you change the mount above, not this variable. It replaced DB_PATH in v4.0.0, when the project stopped being a column and became a file of its own: one database per project, so a backup, a restore and a corruption are all one project's business and never the whole house's. Optional, with /db as the working default in the code, because Unraid does not propagate a new variable to containers that already exist.

Config.Name: SMTP Host
Config.Description: The submission server that posts this container's notifications — mail.smtp2go.com, or whatever service you use. LEAVE IT EMPTY and nothing is ever sent, and nothing complains about it: there is no notifications on/off switch anywhere in this service, on purpose, because two ways to be quiet is one too many and the day the post stops arriving somebody has to work out which of them did it. The two ways are both ABSENCES: no host here, or no address on a consumer. TWO THINGS are posted and no more — a task opened on a person's desk, and a proposal entering the queue, each at the moment it happens. No digest: a roll-up would have to know what is scheduled and when the night's runs have finished, and a container knows neither. At most TEN a day PER PROJECT, and the tenth carries the notice that the sender is paused until tomorrow — that ceiling is not there against twenty mails, which would be information, but against a skill looping on tasks_add and burning a month's allowance in an afternoon.

Config.Name: SMTP Port
Config.Description: Blank uses the port that goes with the security setting: 587 for STARTTLS, 465 for SSL, 25 for none. Set it only if your provider asks for something else. A value that is not a port number BLOCKS startup, at the edge, because a bad number caught at boot is a line with a name on it and caught at the first notification it is a warning nobody is reading.

Config.Name: SMTP Username
Config.Description: The login for the submission service. Leave it empty for a relay that authenticates by IP.

Config.Name: SMTP Password
Config.Description: The password for the login above. Masked here, never written to the log, and never in a message this service builds. A wrong one does not stop the boot — this container does not open an SMTP socket at startup, because that would put its boot at the mercy of somebody else's network — it shows up as a WARNING the first time something is posted.

Config.Name: SMTP Sender
Config.Description: The From address. Required as soon as SMTP Host is set — a message with no sender is refused by every submission service — and that pair is checked at boot. Use an address the service is allowed to send as, or the post leaves and is dropped somewhere you cannot see.

Config.Name: SMTP Security
Config.Description: How the connection is protected. STARTTLS is the ordinary one and what port 587 speaks; SSL is the implicit kind on 465; none is for a relay on the same machine and sends the password in clear, so do not choose it over a network. It is a choice and not something deduced from the port: deducing it would be right until the day somebody runs SSL on 587, and then it would be wrong in silence.

Config.Name: Closing Link Lifetime
Config.Description: How many DAYS the button in a task's email keeps working. Days and not minutes: a one-time code is minted for a gesture about to happen, while a task on your desk waits — five minutes would be a button that is already dead when you read the message on the sofa. After it, the link says it has expired and the task is untouched: it is closed from the log page instead. There is no table of tickets and nothing to clean up — the link carries its own expiry under its signature, and a second press finds the task closed, because closed is closed. The signature is keyed on the project's admin code, so rotating that code voids every link already sent, which is the revocation this design would otherwise not have. Optional, with 14 as the working default in the code.

Config.Name: Backup Directory
Config.Description: Where the administration page writes its copies (VACUUM INTO), one project at a time, from that project's own page. One file per copy, named after the project's slug and the UTC minute — financial-portfolio-20260813T061008Z.db — so the copies of several projects share this directory without meeting. A quiescent copy opens without recovery, and it is the one to take off-site. In WAL mode a database is THREE files, so copying just the .db by hand produces a corrupt backup — use the page. What does NOT end up in here, and it is worth knowing before you carry a copy anywhere: projects.txt, which holds every code in clear. ZFS snapshots remain the main safety net, and they DO take it; this is the copy that leaves the house, and it cannot open a project on its own.

Config.Name: One-Time Code Lifetime
Config.Description: How many minutes a one-time authorisation code stays good for. Modifying anything that already exists — a perimeter, a retirement, a rename, a brief, a group's membership, a project's queue cap — costs the admin code AND one of these, minted on the project's own codes page and copied by hand into the conversation. It is shown once, it burns inside the transaction of the gesture that SUCCEEDED, and a refusal rolls back without consuming it. Five minutes is the default: long enough to paste, short enough that a code left in a scrollback is already dead. Optional, with that default in the code, because Unraid does not propagate a new variable to containers that already exist. A value that is not a positive whole number BLOCKS startup — validated at the edge, where it is one line with a name on it instead of a traceback in a browser at the first minting. The proposal ceiling is NOT here: it is queue_cap, policy of each project, kept in that project's database, because this container is multi-tenant.

Config.Name: Public URL
Config.Description: The full public URL the client uses to reach the service, e.g. https://host.your-tailnet.ts.net (no trailing slash). It must be https and must match EXACTLY what is registered in the GitHub OAuth application, scheme included: the callback there must be BASE_URL + /auth/callback. This is the most common first-run mistake. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: GitHub Client ID
Config.Description: Client ID of the GitHub OAuth application. Create it at github.com under Settings, Developer settings, OAuth Apps, New OAuth App: Homepage = BASE_URL, Authorization callback URL = BASE_URL/auth/callback. USE A NEW APPLICATION FOR THIS SERVICE: do not recycle another container's, or the two will fight over the callback. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: GitHub Client Secret
Config.Description: Client Secret of the same OAuth application. GitHub shows it ONCE, at generation time: if you lose it there is no recovery, you generate another and update it here. Startup is BLOCKED while this still reads CHANGEME.

Config.Name: Allowed GitHub Login
Config.Description: The only GitHub username allowed in. Anyone else who completes the login is refused on every MCP request, the handshake included, so from v1.2 they cannot even list the tools. This is the real front door: the project codes keep projects from finding each other by accident, they do not keep strangers out. Startup is BLOCKED while this still contains CHANGEME.

Config.Name: JWT Signing Key
Config.Description: The key the service uses to sign and encrypt the tokens it issues. GENERATE IT WITH: openssl rand -hex 32 (64 hex characters). It must stay STABLE over time: change it and every issued token becomes invalid, so you must disconnect and reconnect the connector. A different key per service, never reused, never regenerated out of habit. Startup is BLOCKED if it is shorter than 32 characters OR if it still looks like a placeholder — length alone was not enough, because a 64-character placeholder walked straight through and only failed at the first login.

Config.Name: Port
Config.Description: The listening port inside the container, and the same one the Funnel must publish (see Tailscale Serve Port below: the two MUST match, or preflight blocks startup). A different port per service if you run more than one.

Config.Name: Allowed IP Ranges
Config.Default: 160.79.104.0/21 # documented egress of the model provider
Config.Description: Defence in depth: a request is accepted only if its source IP falls inside one of these ranges. It does NOT replace OAuth, it adds to it. Since v1.2 the check runs on every MCP request and not only on tool calls, the handshake included — so a range that is wrong no longer shows up as a call that fails, it shows up as a connector that will not connect at all, and the line in the log saying which source was turned away is what tells that apart from a broken deployment. It does not cover the OAuth routes themselves: whoever is outside these ranges can still complete a login, they simply cannot speak MCP afterwards. SYNTAX: a semicolon separates the entries, a hash opens a description that runs to the end of the entry — the separator is not a comma exactly so that a description may contain one. Example: 160.79.104.0/21 # model provider egress ; 100.64.0.0/10 # tailnet, for a client of your own. An EMPTY string disables the filter entirely, which is useful only while testing locally. A malformed entry BLOCKS startup instead of being skipped: a filter wider or narrower than you believe is the kind of failure nobody notices, so preflight refuses to start and the log prints what it UNDERSTOOD, not what it was given. The older name ANTHROPIC_CIDR is deprecated but still honoured.

Container.Config: 160.79.104.0/21 # documented egress of the model provider

Config.Name: Log Level
Config.Description: How much the service says about itself. It governs ONLY this service's own logger, and that limit is the point: the root logger stays at WARNING, so a library never starts talking on our behalf; uvicorn's access log is pinned at WARNING as well, because one line per request slowly becomes a record of who asked what and when, and the arguments here are project codes; and fastmcp's own logger follows FASTMCP_LOG_LEVEL, which is set inside the image. INFO prints, once, what was found at boot: the registry line, which names the registry FILE and how many projects it serves, and the startup line, which carries this version, the engine's, and the whole resolved configuration. The startup line is what you read to confirm that an update actually took, so WARNING is the quiet setting for a service you have already watched come up. INFO also prints ONE line for every call a tool turns away — 'refused <tool>: <why>' — which is the thing to read the day somebody says the registry is refusing them, and the reason those refusals no longer arrive as thirty lines of traceback. That line carries consumer names, domains and malformed IDs — checked, not assumed: no project code and not the text that was searched for. It is not an access log even by accident, because it records only the calls that did NOT happen, which is useless as a register of what was consulted and is exactly what you need when diagnosing. Project codes do reach the log by another door that this knob does not close: fastmcp logs invalid arguments itself, at WARNING, with the arguments in the line. WARNING silences it, along with the two boot lines, and leaves everything that is a warning proper: the gate turning a stranger away, a wrong admin code, a schema REBUILT at open — rebuilt, never migrated: from v4.0.0 a database of another schema generation is refused by name and the service does not start — a project database created empty, and a LOG_LEVEL that had to be corrected. It does NOT silence the preflight, which prints on stdout and never passes through this logger — a run that fails still says why, whatever this is set to. And it never silences a FAULT: a broken machine keeps its full traceback at ERROR, which is the whole reason refusals and faults are told apart in the code rather than by how their message reads. The list is closed on purpose, at both ends and for different reasons. Below INFO there is nothing to switch on: this code contains no debug line at all, so DEBUG would behave exactly like INFO, and a knob that does nothing gets read as a knob that is broken. Above WARNING the gate's refusals disappear — and since v1.2 the gate covers the handshake, so that line is the only thing that tells a stranger turned away apart from a broken deployment: at the client the two look identical, the connector will not connect. The list is closed in the CODE too, not only in this dropdown, because a container built by hand has no template. Anything that is not INFO or WARNING falls back to INFO and says in the log what it rejected; WARN is understood as WARNING, since Python defines it as an alias and whoever writes it is asking for less noise, not more. A field left EMPTY is not a wrong value and is not reported: it means the same as not setting one, which is INFO. It has to fall back rather than refuse, because setLevel() raises on an unknown value and does so at import — that is, after the preflight has already printed a clean sheet, which is the worst place in the whole startup for a typo to land.

Config.Name: Web UI Port
Config.Description: The port the administration UI listens on INSIDE the container. Leave it empty and it is 9443, which is the value the code carries: a variable born later than its container has to have a working default, because Unraid does not propagate new variables to installations that already exist. If you change it, change the port mapping above to match — they are two halves of one decision, and the half you forget is the one that makes the page unreachable. Startup is BLOCKED on 443, 8443 and 10000: those are the only three ports Tailscale Funnel can publish, the Funnel runs in this container, and on one of them this page would be on the internet instead of on your LAN. Startup is also blocked if it is the same as the MCP port, because the second server to bind would die after the startup line had already said everything was fine.

Config.Name: Web UI Password
Config.Description: The password of the administration UI — the page where proposals are approved, one-time codes are minted and backups are taken. It is typed in a browser and never leaves it: NO TOOL carries it, and that is the shape of 'what is catastrophic has no tool'. It was called WEB_MASTER_CODE up to v3.1.0 and the name changed with the thing it opens: there is no 'master' level any more, there is a UI with a door. If you are updating an existing container, this is a NEW field and Unraid does not carry the old master into it — whatever it shows, put the value in yourself, or the container will not start. Minimum 12 characters; put it in your password manager, because there is no way to recover it and no second account. It is asked for at sign-in, and asked for AGAIN on every gesture that writes — deciding a lot, renewing, promoting, minting a code — once per gesture and never once per rule, because a password typed four times in a row is typed without looking. Backups and the log page do not ask again: a VACUUM INTO changes nothing, and a password retyped where it defends nothing only teaches the hand to type it without looking. Startup is BLOCKED while this is missing or still reads CHANGEME: without it the approval page would be open to whatever reaches the port.

Config.Name: HTTP Mode
Config.Description: How this server speaks HTTP to the client. STATEFUL is the legacy shape: an `initialize` handshake, an Mcp-Session-Id carried on every following request, and a GET stream on /mcp. STATELESS drops all three — each request is served on its own and /mcp keeps only POST and DELETE. What stateless does NOT do is stop a connection from dying: if the cause is underneath, in the tunnel, the request in flight dies either way, and nobody has proved it cures anything. What it removes is the SHARED STATE, and that gain is real: a dropped call costs one call instead of a session to resynchronise, and the retry is clean. For a server that never speaks first — no notifications, no sampling, no subscriptions — a session buys nothing and can only break. The list is closed in the CODE as well as in this dropdown, because a container built by hand has no template, and a value that is neither falls back to stateful SAYING SO in the log rather than refusing to boot: a service down for a spelling mistake in a knob that has a working answer is worse than the mistake. The DEFAULT IN THE CODE is stateful, which is what every version before 4.0.0 did, so a container that never sets this behaves as it always has; this template ships stateless, which is the choice for an installation made today. The two are not in contradiction. The value is passed EXPLICITLY to the server, so fastmcp's own FASTMCP_STATELESS_HTTP cannot put the service in a mode this template does not name. Whatever you choose, the startup line in the log says which one is actually running — that line, and nothing else, is what to believe.

Config.Name: Bind Host
Config.Description: The interface the server listens on inside the container. Leave it as 127.0.0.1: legitimate traffic arrives from the Funnel, which runs in the same container. Setting 0.0.0.0 exposes the service to the LAN without the Funnel's filtering.
